text: Throughout the Spring 2025 semester, I worked with another student to construct and validate a single-phase AC to 3-phase AC converter for the Streamlining Wind Turbines Collaboratory Project
Mechanical Design, Electronics Design, Sustainability, Validation, Teamwork, Machining
WindAid Institute (Peru), Messiah University Collaboratory for Strategic Partnerships and Applied Research

"It would be beneficial to the Streamlining Wind Turbine (SWT) team to create a system that generates 3-phase AC power to simulate power coming from a turbine. With this simulated power, the Turbine Monitoring System (TMS) and the battery can be tested in a controlled environment. Additionally, this interior test design will be quicker to set up and easier to control different power inputs to the system."

These images demonstrate the main goal of the TTS, using an AC motor (top right) to drive a 3-phase AC generator (bottom right). The red tape in the large picture is the rear of that generator, so as the motor spins, the generator, which is held concentric by the boards, can produce power. This whole system was built for less than $30. Below is our test stand design record.
Here shown is the testing setup and results, confirming the capacity to deliver above 300W, not yet meeting our criteria for use.

My primary contribution to this project was the design of the adapter plate between the motor and generator. Since the goal was to build this stand using existing hardware as much as possible, I opted to attempt to use the blade attachment bracket already on the generator and the V-belt pulley that was attached to the motor. This required drilling three holes through the pulley, which would then have standoffs run through them to provide a rigid connection. Unfortunately, while assembling this system the first time, the old pulley warped considerably, so a new part needed to be bought to replace it.

Once this system was attached, there was still a great deal of stress on the system since we could not reasonably make our setup completely concentric. To mitigate this issue, I introduced some intentional play in the bolts interfacing the adapter that would allow limited movement without resistance normal to the axis of rotation. This final design, as shown in the results plot above, only makes about 300W, with 500 needed to accurately simulate the generator that will be on the final version, yet still likely powerful enough to perform preliminary testing.
